This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)+1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{2x\cancel{({x}^{2}+1)}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$
